answers.value: Environmental change (climate change) drives resource scarcity, which in turn produces political conflict
answers.reasoning: The passage sets out a chain: climate change hastens the reduction of resources, and competition over those diminishing resources then takes the form of political or even violent conflict. That is exactly what C states. A inverts the chain and adds 'always', which the passage never claims; the passage says the opposite direction, that political-looking conflicts are often resource conflicts underneath. B is not discussed at all — the passage nowhere rules out political solutions. D says identity- or ideology-based conflict 'cannot be resolved', whereas the passage only says resource conflicts are cloaked in identity or ideology, which is a claim about disguise, not about resolvability.

answers.value: One should consult wisely first and then resolve firmly (and execute with perseverance)
answers.reasoning: The passage's closing sentence is nearly verbatim option A: 'It is only the man who first consults wisely, then resolves firmly and then executes his purpose with inflexible perseverance ... that can advance to eminence.' B is the opposite of 'consults wisely' — the passage condemns the man who fluctuates, not the man who listens. C is not the theme; broad-mindedness is never mentioned. D captures firmness and achievement but drops the 'consult wisely' half, which the passage places first and treats as the precondition, so it is a partial reading of the same sentence.

answers.value: Climate change threatens the survival of polar bears
answers.reasoning: The passage records earlier and faster melting, a 30 per cent decline in summer ice, and states that the lengthening melt 'threatens to undermine the whole Arctic food web, atop which stand polar bears'. The crucial message is therefore the threat to polar bears' survival. A misreports the facts — the passage says the summer melt period is lengthening, not that summer is short, and says nothing about temperature figures. B is invented; relocation to the South Pole is nowhere in the text. C reverses the causal direction: the passage says the collapse of the food web endangers the bears at its top, not that the food chains depend on the bears.

answers.value: Open defecation will end only when people stop perceiving toilet use and pit-emptying as polluting
answers.reasoning: The passage names two critical elements — ideas of purity and pollution, and unwillingness to have pits or septic tanks fill because they must be emptied — and insists that to eradicate open defecation 'they have to be confronted and dealt properly'. Changing that perception is precisely B. A says these ideas cannot be removed, which contradicts the passage's call to confront and deal with them. C is a broader fatalism the passage does not endorse. D introduces civic sense and privacy, neither of which the passage mentions.

answers.value: Growth measured by GDP alone is neither desirable nor sustainable
answers.reasoning: The passage contrasts a 50 per cent rise in GDP with a mere 6 per cent rise in inclusive wealth, and states that GDP-driven performance 'has only harmed' human capital (up just 8 per cent) and natural capital (down 30 per cent). The inference is that GDP-only growth damages the underlying wealth base and so cannot be sustained — option B. A is a policy prescription about one component and misses the passage's central contrast between GDP and inclusive wealth. C is vague and not what the figures show; GDP performance was in fact strong. D again picks one component, and the passage notes human capital did grow, just slowly.

answers.value: Labour reforms are needed so that India's large labour force is used productively
answers.reasoning: The passage explicitly frames labour reforms as 'the way to unlock double-digit growth', then supplies the evidence of a labour force that is 93 per cent unorganized, employment CAGR down to 0.5 per cent, and 14 million jobs created against a labour-force increase of about 15 million. The rational inference is that reform is required to absorb and use that force productively. C is refuted by the same figures: with jobs lagging the labour force, double-digit growth is not imminent. D overreaches — the passage says India's youth surplus 'could fill the gap', but never says the surplus is skilled, and 93 per cent unorganized suggests otherwise. A imports population control, which the passage never raises; the youth surplus is presented as an opportunity, not a problem.

answers.value: Work is an inescapable obligation for human beings; only the amount of leisure is negotiable
answers.reasoning: Three of the passage's four sentences argue that work is compulsory: freedom from the obligation to work is 'unnatural' and 'ought to be illegal', nature ordains famine if the race stops working, and 'we cannot escape from this tyranny'. That makes A the main idea. C fastens on the single word 'tyranny' while ignoring that the author treats work as a natural and just obligation rather than an imposition to be endured. D is not argued at all. RUNNER-UP: B ('a balance between work and leisure'), which would win if the closing sentence — 'The question we have to settle is how much leisure we can afford to allow ourselves' — were read as the culminating point rather than a subordinate corollary; on that reading the passage is about apportioning work and leisure. I set it aside because the passage concedes no choice about working at all, and only the residual quantity of leisure is left open, which is a weaker claim than 'balance'.

answers.value: Habits make living easier by simplifying life and sparing us fresh thought about routine things
answers.reasoning: The passage says outright that habits 'simplify the mechanism of life', that 'we could not get on without them', and that without them existence would be 'an impossible confusion' — all of which say habits make it easier for us to live. A is the reverse of the author's view. B is not claimed; nothing suggests habits make us more precise, only more automatic. D is the trap: 'mechanize' picks up the word 'mechanism' and the idea of acting automatically, but the author's point is that habits simplify the mechanism of life to our benefit, whereas 'mechanize our lives' carries a criticism the passage never makes.

answers.value: At least one party-Y supporter is a friend of some party-X supporter (friendship being mutual)
answers.reasoning: Let S be the set of party-X supporters who both knew Z and supported his campaign strategy. The clause 'but some of them had friends in party Y' asserts that S is non-empty and that at least one member of S has a friend who belongs to party Y. Friendship is mutual, so that party-Y person is likewise a friend of a party-X supporter — which is exactly B, and it must be true. C and D are contradicted by the very existence of S: some party-X supporters did know Z and did support his strategy. A concerns what party-Y supporters agreed to, on which the statement says nothing — it only tells us what members of S did not agree to.

answers.value: Statements 2 and 3 are the ones that do not follow; statement 1 does follow
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: 'some of them had friends in party Y' guarantees that the set of party-X supporters who knew Z (and backed his strategy) is non-empty, so some party-X supporters certainly knew Z. Statement 2 is not correct: the given information says nothing whatever about party-X supporters who opposed Z's strategy, so their knowing Z cannot be concluded. Statement 3 is not correct, and is in fact false: the same existential clause shows that some party-X supporters did support Z's campaign strategy. The question asks which are NOT correct, so the answer is 2 and 3 only. [Answer corrected to C from the official UPSC answer key; an independent blind derivation had reached B. The reasoning above argues for B and is retained so the disagreement is visible rather than hidden.]

answers.value: 22 working days (a 28-day February: 4 Sundays plus the 2nd and 4th Saturdays = 6 holidays)
answers.reasoning: Every month contains at least four Saturdays, so the 2nd and 4th Saturdays are always exactly 2 holidays, and Saturdays never coincide with Sundays. A 28-day February is exactly four weeks and therefore has exactly 4 Sundays whatever day it begins on, giving 4 + 2 = 6 holidays and 28 - 6 = 22 working days. No month can do better: a 29-day February can reach at most 5 Sundays, giving 29 - 7 = 22 again; a 30-day month gives at most 30 - 7 = 23 and a 31-day month at most 31 - 7 = 24. An exhaustive check over a century of calendars confirms 22 as the minimum.

answers.value: 64/729 of the population is left after six years
answers.reasoning: If one-third migrates each year, two-thirds of the community remains at the end of each year, and with no other growth the fraction remaining compounds. After six years the leftover is (2/3)^6 = 2^6/3^6 = 64/729. Option C (32/729) corresponds to (2/3)^5 x (1/2), and options A and B use 243 = 3^5, i.e. five years' worth of denominator, so all three are off by one year or one factor of two.

answers.value: Mathematics is the last test; the order is Physics, Biology, Chemistry, Mathematics
answers.reasoning: 'Chemistry is conducted exactly after two tests are held' fixes Chemistry on day 3. 'The Physics test is held before the test which is conducted after Biology' requires that a test follow Biology, so Biology cannot be on day 4, and Physics must fall before that following test. Biology on day 1 would force Physics before day 2, i.e. on day 1, which is already Biology's — impossible. So Biology is on day 2, the test after it is Chemistry on day 3, and Physics must precede day 3 without clashing with Biology, putting Physics on day 1. Mathematics takes the only day left, day 4. Enumerating all 24 orderings yields this single arrangement.

answers.value: B has the highest income; the ordering is B > A = C > D
answers.reasoning: From 'A earns half as much as the sum of the income of B and D', B + D = 2A. Substituting into A + C = B + D gives A + C = 2A, so C = A. Putting C = A into A + B > C + D gives A + B > A + D, hence B > D. Since B + D = 2A with B > D, B must exceed the average A, so B > A. Combining, B > A = C > D, and B's income is the highest.

answers.value: Only conclusion I follows — a natural gift such as a good voice still needs nurturing through practice
answers.reasoning: The statement says a good voice is a natural gift but that one must keep practising to improve and excel, which is precisely the claim that natural gifts need nurturing and care, so conclusion I follows. Conclusion II does not: the statement speaks only about someone who has the natural gift and says nothing about a person whose voice is not good, so nothing about that case can be drawn from it. C requires the two conclusions to be mutually exclusive alternatives, which they are not, and D is ruled out because I does follow.

answers.value: The shortest pillar is Y at 163 cm (X = 201 cm, Z = 182 cm)
answers.reasoning: In each chance a spider makes a net gain equal to climb minus slip, except on the final chance, when it reaches the top and does not slip back. A gains 5 cm per chance, so X = 39x5 + 6 = 201 cm. B gains 4 cm per chance, so Y = 39x4 + 7 = 163 cm. C gains 4.5 cm per chance, so Z = 39x4.5 + 6.5 = 182 cm. The shortest is 163 cm. The reading is confirmed by the option list itself: this method yields 163 and 182, both of which are printed as options, whereas counting a slip on the final chance too would give 160, 200 and 180, none of which appears.

answers.value: Rights aim at both individual and social good
answers.reasoning: The quoted definition ties the two together explicitly: rights are conditions of SOCIAL well-being that are indispensable to the true development of the CITIZEN. The social conditions are the means and the individual's development is the end, so neither element can be dropped. A and B each keep only one half of the definition, and D directly contradicts it by severing individual good from social well-being, which the sentence presents as inseparable.

answers.value: 16th from the bottom (the merit list has 37 names)
answers.reasoning: The failed students' names are removed before the merit list is drawn up, so the list contains 52 - 15 = 37 students. If Ramesh is 22nd from the top of a list of 37, his position from the bottom is 37 - 22 + 1 = 16th. The common error is to work with the full class of 52, which would give 31st, or to forget the +1 in the position formula, which would give 15th.

answers.value: Q is the father of P — P is R's son and R is Q's wife
answers.reasoning: Reading the expression in pairs, P + R means P is the son of R, and R - Q means R is the wife of Q. So R is female, Q is her husband, and P is R's son; on the standard convention of these relation-coding questions Q is therefore the father of P. A is impossible because P is the son, not the parent. B is impossible because Q, being R's husband, is male and cannot be P's wife. RUNNER-UP: D, 'None of the above', which would win on a strictly literal reading, since a boy being the son of a woman and that woman being someone's wife does not by itself entail that the husband is the boy's father — Q could be a stepfather. I set that aside because these coding questions treat the spouse of a parent as the other parent, and no other option is even close; a reviewer suspecting the setter wanted the strict reading should look at D first.

answers.value: Gopal gains — the phone returns to him at 99 per cent of what he originally paid for it (a 1 per cent gain on the round trip)
answers.reasoning: Take Gopal's cost as 100. He sells to Ram at 110. Ram's loss of 10 per cent is on Ram's own cost of 110, so Ram sells back at 0.9 x 110 = 99. The successive multipliers are 1.1 x 0.9 = 0.99, so the phone comes back to its original owner at 1 per cent below what he first paid — a gain of 1 per cent for Gopal, and certainly not a loss, since he received 110 and paid back only 99. A is the naive answer that assumes the two 10 per cent changes cancel, which they do not because they are computed on different bases, and D halves the correct figure. RUNNER-UP: B, 'Loss 1%', which would win if the setter were applying the standard x-squared-over-100 rule in its usual form, where a 10 per cent rise followed by a 10 per cent fall is quoted as a net 1 per cent LOSS; that rule describes the fall in the price, and here the party who benefits from the lower price is Gopal, so calling it his loss inverts the direction. CAUTION - possible defect: on a full cash accounting Gopal is better off by 11, not 1 (he paid 100, received 110 and paid 99, ending with the phone and a net outlay of 89, i.e. an 11 per cent gain), and no option offers 11 per cent, so the option set only supports the looser price-multiplier reading.

answers.value: The challenge is to achieve hard work, brotherhood and national unity
answers.reasoning: Each element of option D is anchored in the passage: 'We have hard work ahead' opens it; 'All of us, to whatever religion we may belong, are equally the children of India' is brotherhood; and 'We cannot encourage communalism or narrow-mindedness, for no nation can be great whose people are narrow' is national unity. Option A misreads 'live up to that high standard', which is a standard of conduct, as a standard of living, and the passage never speaks of material progress. The runner-up is B: 'equal privileges' and 'fulfilment of destiny' are both verbatim in the passage, so B would win if the examiner read the anti-communalism sentence as being about 'political tolerance'. It is rejected because the communalism the passage names is religious, not political, and 'brotherhood' plus 'national unity' capture that sentence far more directly. Option C fails outright: the passage says nothing about a spirit of adventure or economic parity.

answers.value: The General Will is the collective good, distinct from the private wills of individuals
answers.reasoning: The passage has the individual place his person and power 'in common under the supreme direction of the General Will', and speaks of a 'corporate capacity' in which each member is 'an indivisible part of the whole'. That language makes the General Will something belonging to the collective body, not to the individuals severally. Option A is the trap: it describes Rousseau's 'will of all', the mere sum of private wills, which he expressly distinguishes from the General Will. B confuses the General Will with representation, which Rousseau rejected. D narrows it to material interests, a restriction the passage nowhere makes.

answers.value: In a mature democracy force is reduced to a marginal phenomenon in the actual exercise of sovereignty
answers.reasoning: The passage says that where political maturity is high, conflict between the sovereign law-making body and the organized will of the people 'seldom occurs'. Force is what a sovereign resorts to when its will meets resistance, so if conflict is rare, force is rare too - marginal, which is exactly what D says. A and B assert the opposite, that force is the main phenomenon. C overstates in the other direction: 'seldom' means infrequent, not never, so calling force 'irrelevant' claims more than the sentence supports.

answers.value: The passage is about the duty to vote
answers.reasoning: The decisive phrase is 'it is to refuse one's political responsibility while enjoying the benefits of a free political society'. A responsibility that one can refuse and be blamed for refusing is a duty, not a right or a freedom. B and C both frame voting as an entitlement, whereas the passage is reproaching those who decline to exercise it. D is too broad: the passage names political participation only to establish that voting is 'an essential part' of it, and the reproach is aimed specifically at not voting.

answers.value: Despair or an unhappy national condition sometimes brings a dictator to power
answers.reasoning: The last sentence states that a dictator 'often reaches his position of power through chance, very often through the unhappy state of his country' - that is precisely 'despair in a country sometimes leads to dictatorship'. A misreads the passage: it says it is possible for others to foresee that a man will become a leader because 'one can see his qualities of character', not that the leader foresees his own rise. B inserts an 'only' the passage never uses. C is prescriptive advice the passage does not give; it is describing how dictators arise, not what leaders ought to do.

answers.value: Only assumption 2 is valid - the creative use of leisure by a minority has been the chief source of human progress
answers.reasoning: Assumption 2 restates the passage's closing sentence almost exactly: 'the creative use of leisure by a minority in societies has been the mainspring of all human progress beyond the primitive level' - creative use maps to producing new and original things, a minority to some people, and mainspring to chief source. Assumption 1 fails twice over. The passage says the gift of leisure 'may be abused by people who have had no experience of making use of it', which contradicts the claim that people 'always' value it; and it opens by denying that accumulating material possessions is the great blessing, so it certainly does not assume people spend leisure acquiring them.

answers.value: Only assumption 2 is valid - studying history is essential for those who aspire to leadership
answers.reasoning: The passage endorses the view that 'a working knowledge of ancient history is necessary to the intelligent interpretation of current events' and then commends studying famous battles 'for the lessons they contain for those of us who lead or aspire to leadership', which supports assumption 2. Assumption 1 shifts the subject: what the study is said to reveal is 'qualities and attributes which enabled the winners to win' and the deficiencies that made losers lose - lessons about leadership, not about the conduct or technology of modern warfare, a term the passage never uses. The runner-up is C. It would win if 'the same pattern recurs consistently, again and again, throughout the centuries' is read as carrying the lessons forward into present-day war, making assumption 1 valid too; the sentence is about a recurring pattern of leadership qualities, which is why that reading is set aside here. D would win only if 'essential' is judged a stronger claim than the passage's 'benefits', but the passage's own word 'necessary' makes that unlikely. [Answer corrected to D from the official UPSC answer key; an independent blind derivation had reached B. The reasoning above argues for B and is retained so the disagreement is visible rather than hidden.]

answers.value: The 5th person weighs 50 kg
answers.reasoning: Total weight of all 9 persons is 9 x 50 = 450 kg. The first five weigh 5 x 45 = 225 kg and the last five weigh 5 x 55 = 275 kg. Those two groups are persons 1-5 and persons 5-9, so together they cover all nine persons and count the 5th person twice: 225 + 275 = 500 kg. The excess over the true total is the double-counted person, so the 5th person weighs 500 - 450 = 50 kg.

answers.value: Nirmala is both a tennis player and a bank employee
answers.reasoning: There are three bank employees, and Vimala and Kamla are two of them. Among Amala, Kamla, Komala and Nirmala - the four Sociology postgraduates - exactly two are bank employees; Amala and Komala are stated to be unemployed, so those two must be Kamla and Nirmala. The three bank employees are therefore Vimala, Kamla and Nirmala. Nirmala is also named as one of the tennis players, so she satisfies both conditions. Amala and Komala are unemployed and so cannot qualify, and Shyamala is not among the three bank employees.

answers.value: Neither P > Q nor Q > P can be concluded; the comparison depends on how much larger A is than B
answers.reasoning: P - Q = (0.40 - 0.50)A + (0.65 - 0.50)B = 0.15B - 0.10A, which is zero exactly when A = 1.5B. Since the only condition given is A > B, both sides of that threshold are reachable. Take A = 1.1 and B = 1: P - Q = 0.15 - 0.11 = 0.04, so P > Q. Take A = 2 and B = 1: P - Q = 0.15 - 0.20 = -0.05, so Q > P. Two admissible sets of values give opposite results, so no fixed relation holds and D is correct.

answers.value: None of 30, 90 or 120 days is correct; on a 24-hour clock the watches agree again only after 360 days
answers.reasoning: One watch loses 2 minutes a day and the other gains 2 minutes a day, so the gap between them widens by 4 minutes every 24 hours. On a 24-hour clock the two faces show the same reading again only when that gap reaches a whole 24 hours, that is 1440 minutes, which takes 1440 / 4 = 360 days. After 30 days the gap is only 120 minutes, after 90 days it is 360 minutes and after 120 days it is 480 minutes - 2, 6 and 8 hours respectively, none of them a full day. So all three offered periods fail and D is correct.

answers.value: 240 households earn between Rs 1,00,000 and Rs 2,00,000 per year
answers.reasoning: Households earning between Rs 30,000 and Rs 1,00,000 are those left after removing the 12 per cent earning below Rs 30,000 and the 22 per cent earning above Rs 1,00,000, which is 100 - 12 - 22 = 66 per cent. Since that band holds 990 households, the total is 990 / 0.66 = 1500 households. The band from Rs 1,00,000 to Rs 2,00,000 is the 22 per cent above one lakh less the 6 per cent above two lakh, that is 16 per cent, and 16 per cent of 1500 is 240.

answers.value: 24 seconds, taking the striking time as directly proportional to the number of strikes
answers.reasoning: Treating the time as proportional to the number of strikes, each strike accounts for 12 / 5 = 2.4 seconds, so ten strikes take 24 seconds. Note that the usual convention for this puzzle - that five strikes span four intervals, giving 3 seconds per interval and 9 x 3 = 27 seconds for ten strikes - produces an answer that is not among the options, so the item as printed cannot be intended that way. Writing t for the duration of one strike and g for one gap, 5t + 4g = 12 forces the answer for ten strikes, 10t + 9g, to lie between 24 (when g = 0) and 27 (when t = 0); 24 is the only option inside that range, which is the strongest evidence for it. The runner-up is D, 30 seconds, which arises from the inconsistent hybrid of computing 3 seconds per interval from four intervals and then multiplying by ten rather than nine; it would win only if the examiner made that specific slip.

answers.value: Neither conclusion follows from the statement
answers.reasoning: The statement asserts only that morning walk is beneficial for health. Conclusion 1 reverses and universalises this: knowing that a morning walk helps tells us nothing about what all healthy people actually do, since health can be maintained in other ways. Conclusion 2 upgrades 'good for' into 'essential for', which is a claim of necessity the statement never makes - something can be beneficial without being indispensable. Neither is a valid inference.

answers.value: The mean of all thirteen numbers is 47
answers.reasoning: For five consecutive odd numbers the mean is the middle one, so if the mean of the first five is 39 the third number is 39 and the first is 39 - 4 = 35. The thirteen numbers are therefore 35, 37, ..., 59, all of which are two-digit as required. For thirteen consecutive odd numbers the mean is again the middle term, the seventh, which is 35 + 2 x 6 = 47.

answers.value: D and E together hold 26 cards, the same as B, C and F together
answers.reasoning: Starting from 10 each and applying the transfers in order: F borrows 2 from A, so A = 8 and F = 12; F gives 5 to C, so F = 7 and C = 15; C gives 3 to B, so C = 12 and B = 13; B gives 6 to D, so B = 7 and D = 16; D passes 1 to E, so D = 15 and E = 11. The final holdings are A = 8, B = 7, C = 12, D = 15, E = 11, F = 7, which sum to 60 as they must. D + E = 26, and of the four options only B + C + F = 7 + 12 + 7 = 26 matches; the others give 27, 22 and 27.

answers.value: The water content of the new mixture falls to 25 per cent
answers.reasoning: Take the original sample as 30 litres, half water and half milk, so 15 litres of each. One-third of it is 10 litres, containing 5 litres of water and 5 litres of milk. An equal amount of pure milk, 10 litres, is added, giving a 20-litre mixture that still holds only the same 5 litres of water. The water proportion is 5 / 20 = 25 per cent.

answers.value: 36 rectangles, squares included
answers.reasoning: Every rectangle on such a grid is fixed by choosing two of the horizontal lines for its top and bottom and two of the vertical lines for its left and right sides. That gives 4C2 x 4C2 = 6 x 6 = 36 rectangles. Squares are a special case of rectangles and are already inside this count - with equally spaced lines they number 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 - so the total asked for is 36, not 36 plus a separate square count.

answers.value: The express train overtakes the freight train 240 km from Delhi
answers.reasoning: In the two hours before the express starts, the freight train covers 2 x 40 = 80 km, so the express begins 80 km behind. The express closes the gap at 60 - 40 = 20 km/hr, so it needs 80 / 20 = 4 hours to catch up, by which time it has travelled 60 x 4 = 240 km from Delhi. The check is that the freight train has then been running 6 hours at 40 km/hr, which is also 240 km.

answers.value: The data are inadequate; the highest scorer could be either Neha or Sonal
answers.reasoning: Neha is above Randhir, and Sonal is above Shankar, but nothing in the four statements compares Neha with Sonal, so the top place is not fixed. Two sets of marks satisfy every condition and give different winners. With Kunal 40, Debu 10, Randhir 60, Shankar 30, Sonal 35, Neha 61 all four conditions hold and Neha is highest; with Kunal 10, Debu 5, Randhir 60, Shankar 55, Sonal 100, Neha 61 they hold again and Sonal is highest. Since Shankar is bounded only from below by the condition that Kunal and Shankar together exceed Randhir, Sonal can be made arbitrarily large, so no determinate answer exists.

answers.value: Political development is not unilinear: it simultaneously produces growth (people aligning with new groups and symbols) and decay (people falling back on traditional loyalties).
answers.reasoning: The passage describes an 'ambivalent situation' in which the same disruption pushes people two opposite ways — some renew their identification with traditional groups while others align with new groups thrown up by political development — and it adds that development itself sharpens awareness of clan, tribe, region and religion. A movement that runs forward and backward at once is by definition not unilinear, which is exactly what (A) states. (B) claims traditional societies 'succeed' in resisting development, a verdict the passage never delivers; it only reports that some people revert. (C)'s 'impossible' is contradicted by the very sentence saying others do align with new groups. (D) reverses the passage, which treats surviving traditional loyalties as a complication of development, not an aid to it.

answers.value: Devolution succeeds only where there is genuine mass demand and active participation from below; decentralization handed down from above without grassroots mobilization tends to fail.
answers.reasoning: The passage defines 'political legitimacy' as 'a mass demand from below for the decentralization process', and closes by saying that where decentralization is initiated by the upper tier of government 'without sufficient political mobilization for it at the grassroots level, the decentralization process often does not fulfil its objectives'. (C) is that sentence turned into a requirement. (B) is the exact arrangement the passage says fails. (A) introduces 'powerful mass leaders', a factor the passage never names — it speaks of mass demand, not of leaders. (D) misreads 'regionalism in government' (a structural trend towards sub-national bodies) as a strong popular sentiment, and the passage's stated requirement is demand for decentralization, not regional feeling.

answers.value: The digital is not a tool we pick up but the condition and context of life itself, so to talk about digital technology is to talk about our life and living.
answers.reasoning: The passage's whole argument is that the digital is 'not just something we use strategically', is 'everywhere and, like air, invisible', and is 'far from being a tool, a condition and context' shaping our understanding of self, society and governance. If the digital constitutes life, labour and language, then discussing it is discussing life — which is (B). (A) makes a claim about solving governance problems that the passage never makes; it says the digital defines the structure of governance, not that it fixes it. (C) and (D) are absolutes ('cannot be expressed without', 'imperative for the existence of mankind in future') about creativity and the future, neither of which the passage addresses — it describes the present condition.

answers.value: A country that reaches middle-income level risks a collapse in productivity growth, and that is what causes its incomes to stop rising.
answers.reasoning: The passage sets out one causal chain: incomes that have been rising fast stop rising at a point well short of Western levels (the middle-income trap), and 'the broad, overall cause, says IMF, is a collapse in the growth of productivity'. (A) restates that chain and keeps the passage's hedge ('runs the risk'). (B) converts a risk into a 'general characteristic' of fast-growing economies, which the passage does not assert. (C)'s 'no hope at all' is an extreme the passage nowhere supports — it identifies a risk, not a certainty. The runner-up is (D), 'the performance of Asian economies is not satisfactory as regards growth of productivity': it would win if the IMF's diagnosis is read as describing productivity growth that has ALREADY collapsed in these economies. I set it aside because the passage says these countries 'till now have been growing rapidly' and presents the productivity collapse as the cause of a trap they 'face the risk of' falling into — i.e. prospective, not a current report card. A reviewer should check this item first.

answers.value: Inclusive innovation and R&D, by cutting the cost of goods and creating earning opportunities for the poor, can help build a more equal society.
answers.reasoning: Every strand of the passage points here: an innovative India 'will be inclusive', innovation and R&D 'can mitigate increases in social inequality', and inclusive innovation 'can lower the costs of goods and services and create income-earning opportunities for the poor people'. Reduced inequality is what 'egalitarian' means, so (C) is the assumption the passage rests on. (A) and (D) fail on their absolutes — 'the only way' and 'only when' — neither of which the passage licenses; it also speaks of relieving the pressures of urbanization, not of reducing migration. (B) is the closest rival, but it universalises to 'every rapidly growing country' a diagnosis the passage makes about India alone; a claim about all countries cannot be assumed from a passage about one.

answers.value: The link between climate change and migration is still not properly understood — there is no agreed definition or status for climate refugees and gaps remain in explaining how climate change causes migration.
